connector: You have the theme and two characters. Today you build the comparison paragraph: a theme sentence, evidence from both books, and what makes them alike and different. Build it like a bridge, one board at a time.

a.raw: go now and get into your nightgowns it will be a long night
a.fixed: “Go, now, and get into your nightgowns. It will be a long night.”
a.why: Real words from Number the Stars, Ch. 4: two sentences inside one pair of quotation marks; commas set off now; each sentence starts with a capital and ends with a period.

b.raw: harriet and caspian both had to leave home in the night
b.fixed: Harriet and Caspian both had to leave home in the night.
b.why: Capitals on the two names; no comma needed with one subject and one verb; a period ends it.

end.label: Alike and different, in one sentence

virtue.title: Which pillar is it?
virtue.intro: One more set of moments from this year. Tap the pillar each one shows best.

items.t: Prince Caspian: Peter steps back when Miraz trips, and waits for him to rise.
items.why: He won’t strike a fallen enemy.

items.t: Prince Caspian: Caspian says he doesn’t feel sufficient to be King. “I’m only a kid.”
items.why: He tells the truth about himself.

items.t: Anne of Green Gables: Matthew tells Anne, “It was a girl — my girl — my girl that I’m proud of.”
items.why: He honours what Anne worked for.

virtue.name: pillars

notes.wgrd: Compare themes across texts: name a theme, find it in two books, and say how the characters show it alike and differently.
vocab: The big idea about life that a story keeps showing.
To tell how two things are alike.
To tell how two things are different.
Details from the text that prove what you say.
notes.wordParts: Every base from the year: port, tract, struct, spect, ject, script, rupt, duct, form, press, tain, lev, plus prefixes like pre-, re-, trans-, inter-.
notes.grammar: Spiral review: capitals, commas, quotation marks, complete sentences. Read your sentence out loud and check each mark has a job.
notes.spelling: Spiral review: drop the silent e, change y to i, double the last consonant when the beat is on the last syllable, and spell each word part the same way every time.

transcripts.welcome: Hello again, it’s Opti. Today you build your comparison paragraph. Today’s question: how do you prove two characters share a theme?
transcripts.read: Start with your theme sentence. Then evidence from the first book, then the second. Then say how they’re alike and how they’re different. Use real words from the books as your proof.
transcripts.spelling: Before you hand in writing, check the patterns you know. Did a silent e drop before a suffix? Did a y change to i? Did a consonant double? Check one pattern at a time, and you’ll catch more.
